results.title: Mixed-Method, Multilevel Clustered-Randomized Control Trial for Menstrual Health Disparities | Prevention Science | Springer Nature Link
results.content: # Mixed-Method, Multilevel Clustered-Randomized Control Trial for Menstrual Health Disparities. Given the role of structural factors like healthy food and healthcare access on reproductive health and the grave need for structural interventions to known reproductive health disparities that disproportionately target cisgender women racialized as Black, it is imperative that science begin to examine how structural factors influence menstrual health. Centering those with the greatest need, persons racialized as Black and/or LatinX living in food and healthcare deserts in Northern Manhattan, our illustrative sample includes four groups of persons who menstruate (e.g., cisgender girls and women) that are pre-menarche, pre-parous, postpartum, or perimenopausal. We describe a hypothetical, multilevel clustered-randomized control trial (cRCT) that provides psychoeducation on racism-related trauma and free delivered groceries to both treatment and control groups, while randomizing 30 clusters of housing associations to receive either sexual health clinics at their housing association or free vouchers for healthcare.

results.title: Chapter 3 | Guidance Notes on Evaluation Approaches and Methods in Development
results.content: # Chapter 3 | Guidance Notes on Evaluation Approaches and Methods in Development. Evaluation of International Development Interventions. This chapter presents guidance notes on approaches and methods for evaluators working in international development. The latter are further divided according to their primary function for either *data collection or data analysis*. Finally, each guidance note includes references for relevant background readings (for example, journal articles, book chapters, method guides), illustrative case examples, and, when relevant, other useful resources (for example, links to useful online tools or software). Efficiency Analysis: Cost-Benefit and Cost-Effectiveness. The main reason to do efficiency analysis is to establish whether the benefits of the program outweigh its associated costs. Evaluation questions to be answered by efficiency analysis include the following:. Two main variations of efficiency analysis are *cost-benefit* and *cost-effectiveness* analysis. In cost-benefit analysis, also known as benefit-cost analysis, the program costs and effects are both defined in monetary terms, allowing for a direct comparison of costs and effects.
